business_scope.primary_industry_name: International Air Freight Forwarding and Cargo Aircraft Charter

meta_jurisdiction_context.legal_system_doctrine: Hybrid federal state; Alberta applies the common law tradition (English-derived) with a comprehensive statutory overlay for corporate law (Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c. B-9); Quebec civil law applies elsewhere in the federation and does not govern Alberta corporate entities.
applicable_bilateral_investment_treaties: Canada-United States Tax Convention (1980, as amended by 1995 and 2007 Protocols)
Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)
Canada-China Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement (FIPA, in force 2014)
Convention on International Civil Aviation (Chicago Convention) and Canada-US Open Skies Air Transport Agreement

ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c. 17 (PCMLTFA) and its Regulations, administered by FINTRAC; Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c. C-46, Part VII.1; Special Economic Measures Act, SC 1992, c. 17 (SEMA); Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, SC 2011, c. 31 (JVCFOA); United Nations Act, SC 1991, c. 45; Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c. B-9, Part 16 (Unlimited Liability Corporations) and s. 21.1 (Individuals with Significant Control Registry); Business Corporations Regulations (Alberta), Alta Reg 119/2000 (fee schedule); FINTRAC Guidance on Client Identification, PEP Determination, and Sanctions Screening.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Passport-issuing authority in the country of origin; copies certified by a commissioned notary public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille for documents originating in Hague Convention states; Consular Legalization for non-Hague states

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Conduct / Police Clearance for each director and UBO (country of residence)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Relevant national or provincial police authority
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille or Consular Legalization depending on issuing state

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Notarized UBO Declaration and source-of-wealth attestation substantiating beneficial ownership structure (ISC-compliant information)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public in the UBO's jurisdiction of residence

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank reference letter and source-of-funds confirmation on letterhead of the applicant's depositary bank
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Applicant's existing bank with signature notarized

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Corporate Existence / Good Standing of any foreign parent entity filing an ownership interest in the Alberta ULC
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate registry of the parent entity's jurisdiction of formation

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Duly notarized Power of Attorney appointing Alberta legal counsel and registered agent for the incorporation process
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public in the principal's jurisdiction

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, UBOs (>=25%), authorized signatories, counterparties, and charter principals against: (i) the Canadian consolidated autonomous sanctions list administered under SEMA and JVCFOA; (ii) FINTRAC terrorist-financing prohibitions; (iii) the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) SDN List given the target payment rails (SWIFT USD and Fedwire); (iv) the UN Security Council Consolidated List; and (v) the UK OFSI Consolidated Sanctions List as a banking counterparty norm. Annual re-screening and event-triggered re-screening are required. PEP determination follows FATF Recommendations 12 and 25, with enhanced due diligence for all foreign and domestic PEPs. Cross-border wire transfers >= CAD 10,000 trigger FINTRAC Electronic Funds Transfer Reports; large cash transactions >= CAD 10,000 and terrorist property reports are mandatory. Screening results must be retained in the AML compliance file with timestamps and analyst sign-off.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Corporate Registry System) administered by Service Alberta on behalf of the Registrar of Companies; NUANS name search reports obtained through authorized service providers integrated with the Corporate Registry portal.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must consist of letters of the Roman alphabet and/or Arabic numerals. Non-Roman script names (e.g., Chinese) must be transliterated into Roman characters (PINYIN or equivalent) with a corresponding English translation identified on the NUANS report. The legal element must end the name: for an Unlimited Liability Corporation, the name must terminate with 'Unlimited Liability Corporation', 'ULC', 'U.L.C.', or 'Societe a responsabilite illimitee' (S.R.C.) per ABCA s. 212(1). All words must be correctly spelled and pronounceable; generic geographic qualifiers are permissible but subject to distinctiveness review.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: No extension of an Alberta name reservation is available; on expiry, a new reservation must be filed. If the Corporate Registry refuses a proposed name, the applicant may: (i) within 30 days of refusal, file a written Reconsideration Request with the Director, Corporate Registry, Service Alberta, attaching the original NUANS report, a corrected name variant, and legal submissions on distinctiveness and permissible elements; (ii) if still refused, apply to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta under ABCA s. 22(4) or s. 24 for an order directing the Registrar to issue the certificate of incorporation with the contested name; and (iii) concurrently open a fresh name reservation with a materially distinct distinctive element to avoid delay to the incorporation timetable.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted under the ABCA for the statutory registered office, provided the address is a physical street address located in Alberta that is readily accessible during normal business hours and the registered agent is authorized to accept service of process. However, for an air cargo charter broker seeking IATA Cargo Agency accreditation and Transport Canada Air Cargo Security Program approval, a virtual-only address will attract enhanced commercial-substance scrutiny; a verifiable operating or administrative address is strongly recommended for regulatory inspection purposes.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: High - estimated 55-65% annualized probability of at least one unannounced or announced physical on-site verification within the first 12 months of operation, owing to the security-sensitive nature of international air cargo chartering and the premises-inspection rights of Transport Canada and the Canadian Transportation Agency under the Air Cargo Security Program.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9; ss 9, 12-18 (Articles of Incorporation and Certificate of Incorporation), ss 20-24 (corporate records), ss 100-119 (share capital); Unlimited Liability Corporation designation governed by ABCA with no shareholder limited-liability shield; Alberta company law administered in conjunction with the Personal Property Registry Act for secured filings.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta, Government of Alberta
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form INC-01) filed electronically through an Authorized Corporate Registry Service Provider
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital and no escrow account requirement under the Alberta Business Corporations Act; the authorized share capital may be unlimited or fixed, and paid-up capital is set at the discretion of the incorporators. For a ULC, shares may be issued with nominal or deferred consideration provided the directors record the prescribed consideration in the corporate minute book.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the share subscriptions set out in the Share Subscription List are accepted and that the Subscribers' shares are issued upon full payment of the subscription consideration. RESOLVED, that the registered office of the Corporation be established at the place named in the Articles of Incorporation, Alberta, and that consent to act as registered office be confirmed. RESOLVED, that the following individuals be appointed as officers of the Corporation, to serve at the pleasure of the Board: [full name] President, [full name] Secretary, and [full name] Treasurer. RESOLVED, that the President and Secretary be authorized to execute banking resolutions, open corporate financial accounts, and engage the Corporation's auditors. RESOLVED, that all legal counsel be retained to complete air cargo charter licensing filings.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Name Search and Reservation for the ULC
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta (corporateregistry.gov.ab.ca) and accredited NUANS search houses
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Order a NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) report for the proposed unlimited liability corporation name; verify that the name contains a distinctive element and a legal element, generally 'Unlimited Liability Corporation', 'ULC', or an authorized French-language equivalent; review exact-match and similar-name conflicts with existing Alberta corporations, extra-provincial registrations, and federal entities; submit the Name Reservation Request through an Authorized Service Provider to reserve the name for 90 days.
required_dossiers: NUANS Name Search Report
Name Reservation Request (Form 001)
Signed letter of authorization from the proposed incorporator or shareholder
Proof of proposed ULC name elements consistent with ABCA s 10
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or flagged for confusion with an existing registered name, file a Name Appeal Reconsideration submission with Service Alberta within 15 days; add distinguishing words or a distinctive trademark element; provide a letter of consent from the conflicting name holder and evidence of the applicant's established business usage; a further NUANS report may accompany the resubmission.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Execution of Articles of Incorporation and Director Consents
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Private legal counsel / authorized corporate service provider followed by Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the Articles of Incorporation in the statutory form, specifying the registered office address in Alberta, the classes and maximum number of shares (including the unlimited liability class), the first directors, and any restrictions on business; obtain signed Consent to Act as Registered Office and Consent to Act as Directors from all proposed directors; confirm the resident Canadian director ratio requirement under s 101(3) ABCA (at least 25% of directors must be resident Canadians; special rules apply for wholly foreign-held ULCs); require the incorporator to execute the Articles and complete the Declaration of Compliance.
required_dossiers: Articles of Incorporation (Form INC-01)
Consent to Act as Registered Office (Form)
Director's Consent to Act (Form)
Incorporator's Declaration of Compliance with ABCA
Filing service order confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a notice of deficient filing, cure defects within 30 days by filing amended Articles or corrected consents; rectify director residency ratio by appointing an additional resident Canadian director; if the declaration is questioned, execute a new declaration with corrected statutory citations and resubmit with the revised filing fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Statutory Filing, Payment, and Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry via Authorized Corporate Registry Service Provider (electronic filing window)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upload the executed Articles of Incorporation and consents to the electronic filing portal; remit the statutory incorporation fee (approximately CAD 350 / USD 260) by credit card, debit, or trust account with the service provider; the Registrar reviews for compliance and issues the Certificate of Incorporation; download the Certificate in digital PDF form, verify the corporate name, incorporation date, and Alberta Corporate Registry number; order certified copies and a Certificate of Status for subsequent bank and licensing applications.
required_dossiers: Digitally executed Articles of Incorporation
Statutory fee payment confirmation
NUANS Name Search Report attached in portal
Director consents and registered office consent
Submission checklist acknowledgment
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried or returned, request priority review through the Service Alberta client-support desk and correct all noted deficiencies within the reply period; if the Certificate contains an error, petition for a Certificate of Correction under ABCA s 11; in case of rejected payment, resubmit within five business days to prevent abandonment of the filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Organizational Governance and Corporate Records
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the Alberta ULC and corporate legal counsel
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first organizational meeting or pass written resolutions in lieu of meeting; adopt the First Board Resolution accepting share subscriptions, fixing the registered office, and appointing officers; adopt general by-laws or rely on the ABCA default rules; issue share certificates to the subscribers and record share transfers in the share register; create the corporate minute book with the notice of registered office, director register, officer register, and consent registers; file the initial annual return (if due) and register the beneficial ownership information under Alberta's corporate transparency requirements.
required_dossiers: First Board Resolution / organizational meeting minutes
Share Subscription List and evidence of consideration
Certified Certificate of Incorporation
Bylaws (if adopted by the board)
Bank account resolution and corporate borrowing certificate
Registers of directors, officers, and shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the annual return or transparency filing is rejected, correct the registered office address and director particulars before the statutory deadline; defective officer appointment is cured by a ratification resolution; missing resident-director consent is remedied by obtaining a late executed consent and filing an updated director register with the Alberta Corporate Registry.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Industrial and Operational Licensing for Air Cargo Charter Brokerage
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA), Transport Canada Civil Aviation (TCCA), Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), and the relevant Alberta municipal licensing authority
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply to the Canadian Transportation Agency for an international air cargo charter brokerage licence covering the ISIC 5229 scope; complete the CTA licence application with Schedule A particulars, proof of liability insurance, corporate attestations, and officer background consents; register advance cargo information (eManifest) with CBSA under the Advance Commercial Information program; secure a municipal business licence for the Alberta principal place of business; sign or maintain interline and charter agreements only with carriers holding valid Canadian or foreign air operator certificates; appoint a compliance officer for the AML Program given the Medium-Risk Enhanced banking tier.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation and Certificate of Status
CTA air cargo charter broker licence application and Schedule A
Municipal business licence application
Cargo liability insurance certificate
AML compliance program attestation
Employee and officer background consents for Transport Canada security clearance
CBSA eManifest advance data filing registration
Aircraft charter agreements or broker authority letters from carriers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CTA licence is queried, submit an expedited reconsideration package with the underlying foreign air carrier charter authorization, proof of insurance, and a compliance narrative under Part II of the Canada Transportation Act; if the municipal licence is refused, appeal to the municipal licence appeal board and obtain an interim municipal clearance pending review; for CBSA eManifest rejection, correct the data elements and re-register through the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management portal.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA); Transport Canada Civil Aviation (TCCA) for aviation security and operation; Alberta Transportation and municipal business licensing authorities
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: International Air Cargo Charter Brokerage Licence (CTA) and Foreign Air Carrier Charter Operating Permit

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Office-based air cargo charter brokerage is classified as Exempt from a full Environmental Impact Assessment; a Registration-tier permit is required only if the ULC also operates a freight-handling or warehousing facility exceeding 2,000 m² gross floor area or maintains liquid fuel storage capacity exceeding 2,000 litres, in which case a Step-1 Environmental Site Assessment and licence registration apply.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No industrial wastewater discharge is authorized; all sanitary sewage must be discharged to an approved municipal sewer system per the Alberta Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act and municipal bylaws; volatile organic compound emissions are limited to office cleaning and HVAC refrigerant leakage thresholds under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 Ozone-depleting Substances Regulations (SOR/2016-1120); cargo residue handling must comply with Alberta's Waste Minimization Regulation, and any dangerous goods accepted for air cargo must be segregated and documented under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and Transport Canada TDG Regulations, including Class 3, 6, and 9 threshold limits.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Municipal fire marshal certification under the Alberta Fire Code with an occupancy permit for the registered office premises; structural load inspection certificate for the commercial office space confirming compliance with the Alberta Building Code; Alberta Occupational Health and Safety Code clearance covering workplace hazard assessment, fire-extinguisher availability, first-aid kits, emergency exit signage, ergonomic workstation certification, and noise or ventilation limits under Part 12 and Part 26 of the OHS Code.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC); taxpayer portal: My Business Account (CRA's secure online portal for corporate and GST/HST accounts).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity carrying on business in Canada, including an Alberta Unlimited Liability Company (ULC), must obtain a 9-digit federal Business Number (BN) from the CRA. The BN is the statutory TIN for federal and Alberta-administered tax accounts. Registration is initiated through the CRA's 'Register a Business Account' e-service or by filing Form RC1/RC196 with supporting corporate/foreign registration documents. The entity must activate GST/HST program account (RT suffix) once taxable supplies exceed the CAD 30,000 small supplier threshold, or register voluntarily; an import/export program account (RM suffix) is required for customs transactions. Foreign entities without a permanent establishment may register as non-resident registrants, and may be required to appoint a resident agent or nominee under the Excise Tax Act for service of documents and tax collection. After issuance of the BN, the ULC must file GST/HST returns through CRA's electronic filing channels and corporate income tax returns as applicable.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: An Alberta ULC is generally treated as a taxable corporation under Income Tax Act and Alberta corporate tax law. However, it is eligible for U.S. check-the-box pass-through or disregarded-entity classification for U.S. federal tax purposes, which can create hybrid or transparent mismatches. In Canada, there is no general check-the-box election for federal tax classification, but a taxpayer may elect a non-calendar taxation year under section 249.1, elect under section 216(4) for Canadian rental and royalty income, or file under section 216(1) non-resident election. For GST/HST, non-resident suppliers may elect to use simplified registration procedures or appoint an agent under section 267(1) of the Excise Tax Act. Hybrid mismatch arrangements must be reviewed against OECD BEPS Action 2 and Canada's hybrid mismatch rules in sections 18.4-18.6, with no automatic domestic pass-through election unless the entity is a foreign-owned ULC used for U.S.-style check-the-box planning.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) under the Excise Tax Act; Alberta has no provincial sales tax and applies only the 5% federal GST, while the CRA administers Alberta corporate tax on behalf of the province.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 worldwide taxable supplies in a calendar quarter or over the last four consecutive calendar quarters; once exceeded, mandatory GST/HST registration is triggered. The threshold excludes incidental supplies and supplies of financial services, and a non-resident air cargo charter broker may elect to register voluntarily even below this threshold to claim input tax credits and support zero-rating of exports.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not impose a mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or government pre-approval API for every invoice. GST/HST registrants must issue tax invoices containing the supplier's BN, invoice date, supplier and recipient names, description, tax rate, and tax amount. Electronic invoices are valid if their integrity and legibility are preserved. The CRA requires electronic filing for GST/HST returns for most registrants and accepts EDI or XML formats through trusted service providers but does not operate an invoice-level clearance regime. Customs filing for export goods is governed by CBSA through the Canadian Single Window and the Automated Commercial Environment, including advance cargo information for air cargo; this is separate from indirect tax invoice clearance.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: A supply of goods is zero-rated under the Excise Tax Act where the seller exports the goods and provides documentary evidence of export. Services supplied to a non-resident are generally zero-rated when the non-resident recipient is outside Canada at the time the service is rendered and the service is not related to real or tangible personal property situated in Canada. Air cargo charter brokerage services, including arranging the charter or brokerage of aircraft cargo capacity, may be zero-rated where the service is directly in connection with goods exported from Canada, the recipient is a non-resident, and the service is not supplied to a Canadian resident. The ULC must maintain clear contractual and operational evidence that the charter, freight brokerage, and related logistics services relate to export air cargo and that title or risk passed outside Canada.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CBSA Form B13 or electronic export report in the Canadian Single Window for the air cargo shipment), including the Canadian exporter name, description of goods, air waybill number, and destination country.

Air Waybill (AWB) / House Air Waybill, Bill of Lading, and the cargo charter agreement showing the non-resident shipper or consignee, routing outside Canada, and the nature of the international air cargo movement.

Bank payment and inward remittance evidence, including SWIFT wire or Fedwire confirmation, bank credit advice, or an inward remittance certificate presented by the paying bank, proving the non-resident counterparty remitted the consideration within the prescribed 180-day foreign exchange repatriation and documentation period.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA may reassess zero-rated GST/HST treatment and deny input tax credits or refunds where the taxpayer fails to substantiate actual export and non-resident receipt of services within the statutory audit window. Penalties and interest apply under the Excise Tax Act and Income Tax Act: gross negligence penalties can be up to 50% of the understated tax, knowingly false statements can attract penalties of 10% plus interest on the overstated refunds, and section 285 ETA penalties of 25% may be imposed on improperly claimed refunds. CRA may also use section 323 ETA director liability to collect unpaid GST/HST from directors of the ULC, and if the ULC is treated as a pass-through or transparent entity, CRA may seek recovery from shareholders or beneficiaries. Criminal prosecution may be pursued for deliberate export zero-rating fraud involving forged export or remittance documents.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.mandatory_fx_repatriation_deadline_days_: The 180-day period is applied as the maximum documentary repatriation window for the inward payment to be credited and evidenced before the CRA will allow zero-rating; failure to satisfy this timing may result in a taxable supply reassessment.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (BOC) is the monetary authority; the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) supervises federally regulated deposit-taking institutions; FINTRAC administers the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA). Canada operates no centralized foreign-exchange-control authority; FX transactions are executed through commercial banks under a free-market framework.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Full convertibility exists for both current and capital account transactions. Non-resident investors may freely remit dividends, interest, royalties, and capital proceeds without exchange-control approval. The principal frictions are Part XIII withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (subject to treaty relief) and cross-border reporting of transfers of CAD 10,000 or more under PCMLTFA.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory requirement to surrender, convert, or repatriate export proceeds to Canada. Exporters may maintain foreign currency balances domestically or offshore and convert at market rates. Reporting obligations are limited to statistical trade data to Statistics Canada and record-keeping under tax and AML legislation.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operating and USD Clearing; Escrow available
Provincial Operating Account for Alberta nexus

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility: Low-Medium. A foreign electronic money institution may not operate as a primary Canadian clearing bank without registration as a Money Service Business with FINTRAC. Canadian-dollar settlement on the Large Value Transfer System (LVTS) is only accessible to chartered banks and direct clearing participants. EMIs may serve as supplementary rails for low-value payouts but cannot provide escrow, trade finance, or full liquidity clearing for a ULC air cargo charter operation.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: For a ULC engaged in air cargo charter brokerage, Canadian banks generally mandate that at least one director or a designated Canada-resident corporate representative appear in person for the initial KYC/AML interview at a branch. Remote video verification may be offered to established clients or low-risk structures, but for a new corporate account with non-resident control and unlimited liability, in-branch physical presence is the default requirement. Alberta law permits remote incorporation, yet OSFI and PCMLTFA compliance frameworks make bank-level physical presence binding for medium-risk industries.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial owner of an unlimited liability company with no Canadian physical presence.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified ULC certificate of incorporation and articles, Alberta Corporate Registry transcript, passport and proof of identity of the ultimate beneficial owner, completed beneficial-ownership declaration, independent legal opinion on ULC liability, 12 months of bank statements evidencing source of funds, and completed FATCA/CRS representations.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Aviation-sector flag with high-value cross-border wires to sanctions-sensitive jurisdictions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Transport Canada operating certificates where applicable, ICAO/IATA registration evidence, charter and client contracts, detailed counterparty due-diligence file, OFAC/DFATD sanctions screening reports, independent audit opinions, and commitment to provide airway bills and invoices for each transaction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Fragmented transaction pattern involving multiple third-party payments for fuel, crew, landing and ground handling.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Transaction matrix with aviation-specific identifiers, comprehensive business plan, office lease evidence, bank reference letters, six-month pro-forma cash flow, and a pre-approval list of known commercial counterparties.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Shareholder capital injections should be transmitted via SWIFT MT103/MT202 in the ULC's legal name, using purpose codes X100 or GDIR for direct investment in Canada. The receiving Canadian bank should be given advance notice and documentation, including the share subscription or capital contribution agreement and a Directors' Resolution. The bank will conduct PEP, sanctions, and source-of-funds verification; funds may be credited to the operating account only after compliance clearance. Escrow structures require an executed escrow agreement.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade disbursements flow via SWIFT MT103 for CAD/EUR/USD settlement, Fedwire for USD counterparties in the United States, and the LVTS rail for domestic Canadian-dollar payments. For aircraft charter, lease or large purchase obligations, an irrevocable Commercial Letter of Credit governed by UCP600 may be issued by the Canadian bank. Wire transfer references should always match the underlying charter number or airway bill reference to support audit and sanctions compliance.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) on restricted or illiquid currencies

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (Annual Filing) under Alberta Business Corporations Act (ABCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days of the corporation's anniversary of incorporation date (e.g., if incorporated Oct 1, due by Nov 29 each year)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing results in administrative strike-off risk; the Registrar may dissolve the corporation after 1 year of non-filing. Penalties include loss of certificate of compliance and inability to obtain corporate status documents; directors may face personal liability for continuing operations.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual ISC (Individuals with Significant Control) Register Review and Update
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Maintained in corporate records (not filed with Alberta Corporate Registry unless requested by enforcement)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually within 15 days after any change; no fixed filing date, but must be complete and accurate as of each anniversary
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain ISC register is an offence under ABCA: fines up to CAD $5,000 for directors/officers; repeated non-compliance may support administrative dissolution.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit is required only if the articles, articles of amendment, or special resolution of shareholders require it; or if a shareholder or the Director appoints an auditor under section 208 of ABCA. Private ULCs generally may waive the audit requirement by unanimous shareholder consent for the fiscal year.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) for entities issuing public securities; otherwise ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) under Part II of the CPA Canada Handbook is permitted. For federal tax filings, CRA requires books and records prepared under GAAP (IFRS or ASPE).

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The ISC register must identify every individual with significant control (25% or more of voting rights, any percentage with control rights, or indirect control contracts). Annual review must be done within 15 days of any transfer of shares to confirm/update controlling parties. No annual government filing is required, but the register must be accessible for inspection by the Alberta Corporate Registry upon order.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC)
Minute Book (minutes of shareholders and directors meetings, resolutions, and consents)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: Registered office and Corporate Access Number (CAN) agent services: CAD $350 to CAD $1,200 (approx. USD $260 to $900), depending on service level
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: If an audit is required (e.g., shareholder request or aviation license conditions), typical fee for a small-to-mid-size ULC: CAD $8,000 to $20,000 (approx. USD $6,000 to $15,000)

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Alberta general corporate income tax is 8%, combined with the 15% federal corporate rate for a 23% general combined rate. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation may obtain a combined small-business rate of 11% on eligible active business income within the applicable federal and Alberta small-business limits. A non-resident-owned Alberta ULC is generally a taxable Canadian corporation and is not automatically pass-through for Canadian tax purposes.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Eligible CCPCs may claim the federal small-business deduction and Alberta small-business rate on qualifying active business income. Alberta provides a provincial research and development tax credit for qualifying expenditures, subject to statutory conditions. Federal investment tax credits may apply to qualifying scientific research and experimental development and other eligible expenditures. No general corporate tax holiday applies to an ordinary air-cargo charter broker. Canadian corporate tax treatment does not follow a U.S. check-the-box classification unless a separate foreign-country classification is relevant for foreign tax purposes.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, including applicable schedules and Alberta Schedule 29 or other provincial schedules. File electronically through the Canada Revenue Agency Corporation Internet Filing system or an approved tax-software channel. Alberta corporate tax is administered through the CRA under the federal-provincial tax collection arrangement.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual income tax return; corporate instalments are generally monthly, or quarterly where the corporation qualifies under the applicable instalment rules.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 return is due six months after the end of each taxation year. Any balance is generally due two months after year-end; a qualifying CCPC may generally obtain a three-month balance-due period if the statutory conditions are satisfied. Instalments are due monthly unless a valid quarterly instalment option applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report the legal name, Business Number, corporation type, Alberta jurisdiction, taxation-year start and end dates, address, books-and-records location, and applicable CCPC or non-CCPC status.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-owned ULC must report its Canadian legal status accurately. Ownership by non-residents does not itself make the corporation non-resident if it is incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada under common-law management-and-control principles.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconcile accounting net income to Canadian taxable income by adding non-deductible expenses and deducting permitted amounts, including capital cost allowance, reserves, eligible dividends, and other statutory adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Exclude or separately analyze foreign-source items, non-arm's-length charges, unsupported management fees, charter commissions, and expenses not incurred to earn Canadian-source business income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 8 and capital cost allowance
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Classify depreciable aircraft, equipment, vehicles, software, and other capital property into the correct prescribed class and calculate capital cost allowance within statutory limits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A broker must not capitalize chartered aircraft costs unless it owns or otherwise has a depreciable interest in the aircraft. Payments for aircraft capacity, leases, and brokerage services require separate legal and tax characterization.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclose associated corporations and relevant corporate relationships for allocation of the business limit, specified corporate income, and other rate calculations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose foreign parent entities, sister companies, common-control entities, and entities connected through control or factual influence where the statutory association rules apply.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 23 or applicable CCPC status schedules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Determine whether the corporation is a CCPC, public corporation, other private corporation, or a corporation controlled by non-residents, and apply the corresponding rate and deduction rules.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A ULC owned or controlled by non-residents will generally not qualify as a CCPC. Do not claim the small-business deduction without testing the Canadian-control requirements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 50 and Schedule 9 ownership information
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report shareholder and ownership information required by the T2 schedules, including significant shareholders and associated corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Maintain ownership records, ultimate beneficial ownership information, voting rights, and control agreements for foreign shareholders and related entities.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 125 and Schedule 141 financial statement information
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report income statement items, balance-sheet information, accounting standards, and financial-statement notes in the required format.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile Canadian tax reporting to audited or management accounts and retain a clear allocation of Canadian brokerage revenue, foreign commissions, aircraft-related costs, and intercompany charges.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 5 foreign tax credits and other deductions
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim eligible foreign tax credits, dividends received deductions, and other applicable corporate deductions, subject to limitation by foreign-source income and statutory baskets.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Document foreign taxes paid or withheld on foreign-source commissions and services. A foreign tax credit is not available merely because a foreign payer withheld an amount if the income is not properly included in Canadian income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 21 and loss utilization schedules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report non-capital losses, net capital losses, restricted losses, and utilization against current-year income. Non-capital losses are generally carried forward 20 years and back 3 years; net capital losses are generally carried forward indefinitely and back 3 years, subject to statutory rules.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Track losses by type and taxation year. Loss utilization may be restricted after an acquisition of control or a material change in the business.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 23 and Alberta provincial tax schedules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculate Alberta taxable income, provincial rate components, small-business deductions, credits, and provincial tax payable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income to Alberta using the applicable permanent-establishment and provincial allocation rules. An Alberta registered office alone does not establish that all Canadian income is Alberta income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report relevant foreign affiliates, controlled foreign affiliates, surplus accounts, foreign accrual property income, and related foreign affiliate transactions where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A foreign-owned ULC must assess whether it holds or controls foreign subsidiaries, branches, aircraft-owning entities, or agency entities and whether foreign affiliate reporting is required.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T106 Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report material non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents, including services, commissions, loans, interest, royalties, guarantees, and cost allocations. The principal reporting threshold is generally CAD 1 million of total reportable non-arm's-length non-resident transactions, subject to the form instructions and exclusions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Aggregate transaction categories and retain agreements, invoices, payment evidence, pricing analyses, and counterparty residence information. The T106 threshold is a reporting threshold and does not eliminate transfer-pricing documentation requirements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T1134 Information Return Relating to Controlled and Not-Controlled Foreign Affiliates
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report Canadian-resident corporations' interests in foreign affiliates where the ownership and reporting conditions are met.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The return concerns foreign affiliates of the Canadian corporation and is distinct from the Canadian corporation's foreign ownership by its parent.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T4A, T4, T5, NR4, and GST/HST reporting
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Issue information slips and file related information returns for employees, service providers, Canadian dividends, non-resident amounts, and taxable supplies. Register and file GST/HST returns where the corporation carries on taxable supplies and exceeds registration thresholds.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use NR4 reporting for amounts subject to Canadian non-resident withholding. Confirm whether international freight, arranging, brokerage, and ancillary services are zero-rated, exempt, or taxable under the applicable GST/HST place-of-supply rules.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing generally attracts a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% of the unpaid balance for each complete month late, up to 12 months. A repeat late filer may face 10% plus 2% per month, up to 20%. Interest accrues on unpaid tax, penalties, and instalment deficiencies at CRA prescribed rates. Failure to file T106 or other information returns may attract daily or fixed statutory penalties, depending on the form and applicable provision. Gross-negligence penalties may equal 50% of the understated tax or overstated credit. False statements, deliberate omissions, and tax evasion may create criminal exposure.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The Canadian domestic withholding rate on taxable dividends paid or credited to a non-resident is generally 25%. A treaty may reduce the rate. Under the Canada-United States treaty, the rate is generally 5% where the beneficial owner is a qualifying company holding at least 10% of the voting power, and 15% in other treaty-eligible cases. Treaty entitlement requires residence, beneficial ownership, limitation-on-benefits or equivalent anti-abuse compliance, and satisfaction of the applicable treaty conditions.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The Canadian payer should obtain and retain a valid Form NR301 for treaty-reduced dividends, Form NR302 for qualifying partnerships, or Form NR303 for qualifying hybrid entities, or equivalent reliable documentary evidence. The payee should provide a current certificate or evidence of residence issued by its tax authority where required, identify the beneficial owner, and substantiate treaty eligibility. The payer must withhold and remit the correct amount to the CRA, generally by the 15th day of the month following payment or credit, issue Form NR4, and file the NR4 information return by the last day of March following the calendar year. If treaty entitlement is uncertain, withholding at 25% is the protective position; the recipient may seek relief or a refund through the CRA process.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: The domestic Canadian withholding rate is generally 25% on royalties and similar amounts paid or credited to non-residents, subject to statutory exemptions and treaty reductions. Canada generally does not impose withholding on ordinary arm's-length interest paid to a non-resident, except for specified categories such as participating debt interest, certain related-party interest, and other amounts covered by the Income Tax Act. Treaty rates commonly reduce royalty withholding to approximately 10% and interest withholding to approximately 10%, but rates vary by treaty, payment type, beneficial ownership, anti-abuse provisions, and limitation-on-benefits rules. Charter payments, aircraft leases, commissions, software, know-how, technical services, and freight-related payments must be classified separately; a contractual label does not determine withholding treatment.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canada has no general monetary threshold below which the contemporaneous documentation requirement in Income Tax Act section 247(4) automatically disappears. A taxpayer must prepare or obtain reasonable contemporaneous documentation for non-arm's-length cross-border transactions and provide it to the CRA within three months of a written request. CAD 1 million is principally the T106 reporting threshold for aggregate reportable non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents, not a safe harbor from transfer-pricing analysis. Country-by-country reporting generally applies to a Canadian-resident ultimate parent or surrogate parent of an MNE group meeting the consolidated-revenue threshold of EUR 750 million in the preceding fiscal year, converted under the prescribed rules.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no separate United Kingdom-style Economic Substance Regulations regime. Economic substance is nevertheless relevant through the general anti-avoidance rule, transfer-pricing rules, beneficial-ownership and treaty anti-abuse principles, sham and agency doctrines, foreign accrual property income rules, interest limitation rules, and common-law residence and management-and-control principles. A Canadian ULC must maintain genuine Canadian decision-making, qualified personnel or properly supported functions, commercial records, bank and payment controls, risk assumption consistent with contracts, and evidence that charter-brokerage functions are actually performed. A corporation with only a registered office, nominee directors, circular payments, and no operational capacity faces reassessment, denial of deductions, treaty-rate denial, penalties, and possible recharacterization.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax evasion and false tax reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Concealing brokerage revenue, fabricating charter expenses, using sham invoices, omitting foreign accounts or related-party transactions, or knowingly claiming unsupported deductions or credits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil reassessment of tax, arrears interest, gross-negligence penalty generally equal to 50% of the understated tax or overstated credit, and criminal prosecution. Tax evasion on indictment may result in a fine of up to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded and imprisonment for up to five years; summary-conviction consequences also apply under the Income Tax Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be jointly and severally liable for unremitted source deductions, including payroll and certain non-resident withholding amounts, subject to statutory due-diligence defenses. Personal criminal liability can arise for directing, authorizing, assenting to, or participating in the offence. Civil restitution, asset recovery, and imprisonment are possible; a travel ban is not an automatic tax penalty but may arise from bail, court orders, immigration consequences, or enforcement proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to remit non-resident withholding tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, royalties, interest, rent, software or know-how fees, or other potentially withholdable amounts to non-residents without determining the correct statutory or treaty rate, remitting the tax, or filing NR4 information returns.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The payer may be assessed for the full unremitted amount, arrears interest, failure-to-remit penalties, information-return penalties, and gross-negligence penalties. Directors may be assessed personally under the director-liability provisions for source deductions if the corporation failed to remit and statutory conditions are met.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Personal assessment is possible after statutory collection steps against the corporation, subject to due-diligence defenses. Deliberate withholding fraud may produce criminal charges, restitution orders, seizure, and imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging excessive related-party commissions, shifting charter profits through unsupported management fees, using non-arm's-length aircraft leases, or failing to price guarantees, financing, and agency arrangements at arm's length.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may adjust income under section 247, deny or recharacterize expenses, impose a transfer-pricing penalty generally equal to 10% of the adjustment where the statutory conditions are met, deny penalty protection for inadequate documentation, and impose interest and other penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not ordinarily personally liable merely because a transfer-pricing adjustment is made, but personal liability can arise for knowing participation in false records, fraud, tax evasion, or unpaid source deductions. Civil recovery and criminal imprisonment remain possible for intentional misconduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Routing dividends, interest, or royalties through a conduit entity lacking beneficial ownership, using a treaty jurisdiction without substantive commercial purpose, or submitting inaccurate residence and treaty-status certifications.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Treaty relief may be denied, withholding may be reassessed at 25%, interest and penalties may apply, and the general anti-avoidance rule or principal-purpose anti-abuse rule may be invoked. False certifications may support criminal prosecution.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers who knowingly approve false treaty documentation may face civil recovery, penalties, prosecution, restitution, and imprisonment. Travel restrictions are fact-specific and normally require a court or enforcement basis.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell company and lack of corporate substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining an Alberta ULC as a paper entity with nominee management, no real Canadian functions, circular payments, undocumented agency arrangements, or bank-account activity inconsistent with the stated air-cargo brokerage business.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Potential denial of deductions, transfer-pricing adjustments, treaty-benefit denial, residence disputes, GAAR reassessment, corporate-record penalties, and anti-money-laundering reporting or enforcement consequences. A shell characterization alone is not a standalone offence, but fraudulent or evasive conduct is actionable.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Canadian corporate law generally preserves separate legal personality, but courts and regulators may impose personal liability for fraud, oppression, knowing assistance, breach of fiduciary duty, unlawful distributions, or statutory remittance failures. Veil piercing is exceptional and fact-dependent; imprisonment requires an applicable criminal offence.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML, proceeds of crime, and sanctions violations
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Accepting opaque third-party payments, disguising beneficial owners, processing funds linked to sanctioned persons or aircraft, structuring payments to avoid reporting, or failing to report suspicious transactions where the business is a reporting entity.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act may impose administrative monetary penalties, compliance orders, record-keeping and client-identification obligations, and criminal prosecution. Criminal Code money-laundering offences may carry imprisonment of up to ten years on indictment. Sanctions violations under the Special Economic Measures Act or related legislation can attract substantial fines and imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, officers, and employees may be prosecuted for knowing participation, counseling, aiding, or directing prohibited conduct. Conviction may result in fines, forfeiture, restitution, imprisonment, and asset or travel restrictions imposed under applicable proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Sanctions, export-control, and aviation regulatory breach
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Chartering aircraft for prohibited destinations or counterparties, dealing with blocked persons, transporting restricted cargo, or operating brokerage activities without required aviation, customs, security, or transport approvals.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Possible measures include licence suspension, cargo seizure, administrative penalties, customs assessments, denial of permits, corporate fines, and criminal prosecution under Canadian sanctions, customs, export-control, and aviation legislation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Responsible directors and officers may face prosecution where they authorized or knowingly permitted the breach. Consequences may include fines, imprisonment, forfeiture, director disqualification under applicable law, and court-ordered restrictions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register, charging the wrong GST/HST rate, incorrectly treating taxable brokerage services as zero-rated, failing to remit collected tax, or misclassifying employees as independent contractors.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may assess unremitted GST/HST, source deductions, interest, late-filing and late-remittance penalties, director-liability assessments, and gross-negligence penalties. Persistent non-compliance may result in prosecution.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for unremitted payroll source deductions and certain GST/HST amounts after statutory conditions are met, subject to due diligence. Knowing evasion may lead to fines, restitution, seizure, and imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Improper corporate distributions and insolvency misconduct
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Distributing dividends or repaying shareholder loans while insolvent, stripping assets from the ULC, or paying related parties ahead of tax, employee, or secured-creditor obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Distributions may be voidable or recoverable, directors may face statutory compensation claims, and insolvency, preference, fraudulent-conveyance, and corporate-law remedies may apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face civil restitution, contribution claims, oppression remedies, disqualification, and liability for knowing approval of unlawful distributions. Imprisonment arises only where the conduct also constitutes a criminal offence such as fraud.
